data.text/html:
p-values: what they are and how to interpret them

An interactive companion to StatQuest's "p-values: What they are and how to interpret them" (Josh Starmer).
Drug A cured 37% of people, drug B cured 31%. Is drug A actually better, or did a few weird random things (a rare allergy here, a strong placebo effect there) just land unevenly? The p-value is the number that helps decide.
Color language used throughout: orange = drug A, blue = drug B, red = p < threshold ("significant"), grey = not significant. The notebook follows the video: (1) why one patient isn't enough, (2) the p-value under "no difference" and the 0.05 threshold, (3) choosing other thresholds, (4) what p-values look like when there is a difference, (5) p-values don't measure effect size, plus a bonus on misconceptions and p-hacking, a sandbox, a quiz and a recap.

data.text/markdown:
1 · Why one person per drug tells us nothing

The video starts with one person on drug A (cured, hooray!) and one on drug B (not cured, bummer). Maybe drug B's patient had an allergy, missed a dose, or drug A's patient just had a placebo effect. Weird random things happen, so we need many people. But even with many people, how big must the gap be before we stop blaming chance? To answer that, we compute a p-value for the 2×2 table (here with Fisher's exact test):
cured not cured
drug A ||(a||) ||(b||)
drug B ||(c||) ||(d||)
Pick one of the video's experiments, or set your own true cure rates and run a fresh trial.

data.text/markdown:
2 · The p-value, defined by giving the same drug twice

The video's key move: give drug A to both groups. Now every difference is 100% weird random stuff. Most runs give a large p-value (like 0.9), but every once in a while all the allergic people land in one group and all the strong placebo reactors in the other, and we get p = 0.01. Calling that "different" is a false positive.
A 0.05 threshold means: if there is no difference and we repeat the experiment many times, about 5% of the experiments give ||(p < 0.05||), i.e. a false positive.
Formally, the p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis (no difference) is true, of seeing a difference at least as extreme as the one observed: ||[p = P\big(\,|\text{difference}| \ge |\text{observed difference}| \;\big|\; H_0\,\big)||]Below, each falling dot is one complete experiment (two groups, same drug, two-proportion z-test). It lands in the bin of its p-value. Red dots are false positives.

data.text/markdown:
3 · Picking the threshold: 0.00001, 0.05 or 0.2?

The threshold (often called α) is the false-positive rate you're willing to live with:
situation in the video threshold false positives
it's extremely important to be right 0.00001 1 in 100,000 experiments
the usual default 0.05 1 in 20
"will the ice-cream truck be on time?" 0.2 2 in 10
0.05 is popular because pushing false positives below 5% "often costs more than it's worth" (more people, more money). Click the α buttons in the simulator above; the table below re-scores the same simulated experiments at every threshold.

data.text/markdown:
4 · When there is a difference: p-values pile up near 0

Section 2 gave the same drug twice (||(H_0||) true) and p-values came out flat. What if drug A really is better (||(H_1||) true)? Then small p-values become common, and the share of experiments with ||(p < \alpha||) is the test's power: the chance of correctly detecting a real difference. ||[\text{under } H_0:\; p \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1) \qquad\qquad \text{under } H_1:\; p \text{ piles up near } 0 \;(\text{more so with bigger effects and more people})||]Overlay: grey = same drug (||(H_0||)), orange = drug A truly better (||(H_1||)).

You can't tell the worlds apart.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eUse the video's \u003cstrong\u003e6-point\u003c/strong\u003e difference with ~200 people per drug: power is only ≈ 25%, so p ≈ 0.24 (the video's result) is very plausible\n   \u003cstrong\u003eeven though drug A really is better\u003c/strong\u003e. \"Not significant\" ≠ \"no difference\".\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eKeep 6 points and push people to 1000: the orange pile slams against 0.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5 · p-values do not measure effect size

The video's final (and most interesting) point: a small p-value tells us drug A is probably different from drug B, not how different. The p-value mixes two things: the size of the difference and the amount of data.
  • 6-point difference, few people → p = 0.24 (not significant)
  • 1-point difference, lots of people → p = 0.04 (significant!)
Drag the A and B markers to set the observed cure rates. The difference updates instantly; release to recompute p-values across sample sizes.

Slide n up to 1000: now p is tiny. \u003cstrong\u003eThe effect didn't change; only the data did.\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eDrag B to 36% (a 1-point gap) and set n = 20,000: p ≈ 0.04, \"significant\" for a difference nobody may care about.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSo always report the \u003cstrong\u003eeffect size\u003c/strong\u003e (and ideally a confidence interval) next to the p-value.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
6 · Bonus: misconceptions and p-hacking

The video doesn't cover this section, but it follows from section 2: if 5% of no-difference experiments are "significant", then running many of them is a reliable way to manufacture a finding. What a p-value is NOT
Misreading Why it's wrong
"p = 0.03 means a 3% chance the drugs are the same" p is computed assuming they're the same. It's P(data this extreme | ||(H_0||)), not P(||(H_0||) | data).
"p = 0.24 proves the drugs are the same" Section 4: with low power, real differences often give large p. Fail to reject ≠ accept.
"p = 0.0001 means a huge effect" Section 5: tiny effects + lots of data give tiny p.
"p < 0.05 means the result will replicate" With 5% false positives and low power, many "findings" don't.
p-hacking = trying analyses until something gives p < 0.05. Two classic ways:
  1. Many outcomes (the "jelly bean" problem): test 20 things that don't work; at α = 0.05, ||(P(\text{at least one } p<0.05) = 1 - 0.95^{k}||), which is 64% for ||(k = 20||).
  2. Optional stopping: check the p-value after every new batch of patients and stop as soon as p < 0.05.

Set k = 20 and re-roll: most studies \"discover\" something. Every red bar is a false positive.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eIn optional stopping, set peeks to 1 (≈ 5%), then 20 (≈ 20%+). Each peek is another lottery ticket.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eThe cure is boring: \u003cstrong\u003edecide the outcome, sample size and α in advance\u003c/strong\u003e, and correct for multiple tests.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
7 · Sandbox: analyse your own 2×2 table

Type in any experiment (drugs, A/B tests, ad clicks). You get the p-value and the effect size with a 95% confidence interval, so you never report one without the other.
